headline: A Proposal to Translate Neural Activations Into Human-Readable Language
lede: In September 2022, Ilya Sutskever proposed something deceptively simple: apply neural machine translation to the activations inside a neural network, treating what a model computes internally as a foreign language to be decoded into human text. The idea specified both supervised and unsupervised variants — and it anticipated the two main directions that automated interpretability research would take over the following two years. Sutskever went on to co-author both of OpenAI's major papers in this area.
body:
In September 2022, Ilya Sutskever, then chief scientist of OpenAI, put forward a new approach to *mechanistic interpretability* — the effort to reverse-engineer what a neural network actually computes, as opposed to merely observing its outputs. His idea: apply *neural machine translation* to the activation patterns inside a network, treating the machine's internal states as a foreign language to be decoded into human text. The proposal specified both supervised and unsupervised variants, and it anticipated the two main directions the field would take over the following two years.

The problem it addresses is that a single neuron in a large transformer can respond to concepts as unrelated as Olympic athletes, prime numbers, and a specific Japanese honorific — a phenomenon called *polysemanticity*. Anthropic's *Toy Models of Superposition*, published the same month as the tweet, showed why: **models encode far more concepts than they have neurons**, cramming multiple features into shared activation directions through a process called *superposition*. Making networks legible requires first disentangling those compressed representations before any translation can begin.

No published work has trained a literal NMT architecture on raw activations. The field instead converged on two approaches that each implement half of Sutskever's sketch. *Sparse autoencoders* (SAEs) — dictionaries trained to decompose activation vectors into many sparsely-firing directions — handle the unsupervised side: Anthropic's 2023 *Towards Monosemanticity* extracted over 4,000 interpretable features from a one-layer model, and by 2024 the technique scaled to Claude 3 Sonnet, surfacing features associated with deception and dangerous content. On the supervised side, OpenAI's May 2023 *Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language Models* — with Sutskever listed as a co-author — used GPT-4 to auto-generate and score natural-language explanations for all 307,200 neurons in GPT-2; peak explanations achieved roughly 10% correlation with actual firing patterns.

The closest literal implementation of the translation framing is the *Tuned Lens* (2023), which trains a learned affine probe at each transformer layer to map intermediate hidden states into vocabulary-space — decoding what the model appears to predict at each processing step, layer by layer. A December 2025 paper pushed closer still: researchers trained a model to reason in ROT-13, then used activation probes to recover the hidden reasoning without supervision, demonstrating that translation from activation-space to language-space is technically feasible. A harder test came from January 2025 work that attempted to replace a transformer's feedforward layers entirely with LLM-generated natural-language descriptions of each neuron; the substitution failed to preserve model behavior, marking the current ceiling of explanation fidelity.

Sutskever is co-inventor, with Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le, of the *seq2seq* encoder-decoder architecture that underpins modern NMT — which lends his framing the precision of an inventor repurposing his own tool. His co-authorship on both of OpenAI's subsequent automated interpretability papers suggests the post was less a casual observation than the opening note of a research agenda. **The question it leaves open** is whether activation space has cross-layer, cross-position structure — something like a grammar or syntax — that piecemeal neuron-by-neuron explanation systematically misses, and whether a translation architecture trained end-to-end on activations would recover it.

concepts.definition: The effort to reverse-engineer the computations inside a neural network — specifying what algorithms and representations it has learned — rather than just describing its input-output behavior. The goal is a human-understandable account of what the network is doing at each step, not merely what answers it produces.

A deep-learning approach to translating text between languages. An encoder compresses the source sentence into a dense vector; a decoder generates the target-language sentence from that vector. The technique underpins most modern translation services and is the original domain of the seq2seq architecture.

The property of a single neuron firing in response to multiple distinct, unrelated concepts. A polysemantic neuron might activate for optical illusions, Roman numerals, and a specific actor — making it impossible to assign any single human-interpretable meaning to it.

The hypothesis that neural networks represent more distinct concepts than they have neurons, by encoding multiple features as overlapping directions in the same activation space. It is the root cause of polysemanticity and a central obstacle to interpreting individual neurons: you cannot read off a single concept from a neuron that encodes several.

Neural networks trained to reconstruct their input while activating only a small fraction of their hidden units at once. When trained on a larger model's activations, SAEs tend to learn a large dictionary of interpretable directions — one direction per concept — disentangling the superposition that makes raw neurons opaque.

An encoder-decoder architecture introduced by Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le in 2014 that maps an input sequence to an output sequence of potentially different length. It became the foundation for neural machine translation and is the architecture Sutskever proposed — by analogy — for decoding activation sequences into human language.

A mechanistic interpretability method that trains a small learned affine probe at each transformer layer to map that layer's hidden state into the model's output vocabulary space. The technique lets researchers read off what the model appears to be predicting at each intermediate processing step, treating each layer's activations as a dialect to be translated.

The numerical output of a neuron or layer given a specific input. Activations are the intermediate representations a network computes as it transforms input into output. In interpretability research they are the raw signal to be decoded — analogous to the source language in Sutskever's NMT framing.

In mechanistic interpretability, features are the atomic units of representation: directions in activation space that correspond to identifiable human-interpretable concepts, such as 'this token is part of a Python function' or 'the text involves financial fraud.' A key goal of the field is to find a basis in which features are sparse and monosemantic.

The dominant neural network architecture for large language models, introduced in 2017. It processes sequences using self-attention — a mechanism that lets every token directly influence every other token — stacked in many layers that alternate attention with feedforward networks.

A two-layer neural network component applied to each token independently within each transformer layer, after the attention step. FFN layers are thought to store factual associations and memorized patterns; they are a primary target of mechanistic interpretability work.

A trivial letter-substitution cipher that shifts each letter 13 positions in the alphabet (applying it twice returns the original). Researchers used it to make a language model reason in an artificial hidden language, creating a controlled test of whether activation probes could decode concealed reasoning without supervised labels.

sources.title: Language Models Can Explain Neurons in Language Models (OpenAI, May 2023)
sources.note: Primary implementation of supervised verbalization of activations; Sutskever is a co-author

sources.title: Toy Models of Superposition (Anthropic, Sep 2022)
sources.note: Published same month as the tweet; establishes why polysemanticity and superposition emerge

sources.title: Scaling and Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders (OpenAI, Jun 2024)
sources.note: OpenAI's SAE work scaled to GPT-4; Sutskever again a co-author

sources.title: Towards Monosemanticity (Anthropic, Oct 2023)
sources.note: Key SAE breakthrough extracting 4,000+ interpretable features from a one-layer model

sources.title: Scaling Monosemanticity (Anthropic, May 2024)
sources.note: SAE approach scaled to Claude 3 Sonnet; feature steering and safety-relevant features demonstrated

sources.title: Interpreting the Second-Order Effects of Neurons in BERT / Tuned Lens (Mar 2023)
sources.note: Closest NMT-style approach: learned per-layer probes translate hidden states to vocabulary-space

sources.title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency (Oct 2023)
sources.note: Supervised direction-extraction from activation space; implements the labeled-contrast side of Sutskever's proposal

sources.title: Unsupervised Decoding of Encoded Reasoning Using LM Interpretability (Dec 2025)
sources.note: Most literal test of unsupervised activation translation; uses ROT-13 reasoning as ground truth

sources.title: Partially Rewriting a Transformer in Natural Language (Jan 2025)
sources.note: Negative result: replacing FFN layers with NL explanations fails; marks current ceiling of explanation fidelity

sources.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models (EleutherAI, Oct 2024)
sources.note: Open-source pipeline for auto-verbalizing SAE features at scale; five new scoring metrics

sources.title: Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety: A Review (TMLR, Apr 2024)
sources.note: Authoritative survey defining the field and its core concepts

sources.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits (Anthropic, Dec 2021)
sources.note: Foundational paper for circuit-level interpretability underpinning all subsequent work
